summary: Discusses how the Path Computation Element applies to point-to-multipoint traffic engineering in MPLS and GMPLS networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A planner who finds routes can also plan routes where one sender reaches many receivers. This talks about that.

subtitle: Computing paths for traffic reaching multiple destinations in MPLS networks

tldr.problem: Routers that originate point-to-multipoint traffic-engineered paths lack the processing power to compute optimal trees reaching many destinations while maintaining control plane stability.
tldr.mechanism: The Path Computation Element architecture offloads P2MP path computation to dedicated servers or high-capacity routers that use sophisticated algorithms to select branch points and paths, or fragment computation across multiple PCEs.
tldr.outcome: Networks can support dynamic multipoint delivery with optimal routing and fast failure recovery without overloading routers.

today: RFC 5671 is an Informational document that remains relevant as a reference for P2MP path computation applicability. The PCE architecture has evolved with extensions for P2MP support, including communication protocol enhancements in later RFCs. It is widely referenced in traffic engineering discussions involving multipoint delivery.

sections.title: The Point-to-Multipoint Challenge
sections.content:
In packet networks, point-to-multipoint (P2MP) delivery means one source sends to multiple destinations. In traffic-engineered MPLS networks, such paths must be computed with constraints on the resources they use, and the computation is complex. The source router must choose branching points in the network—routers that split the path into separate branches toward different destinations—and optimize the tree shape to minimize cost, latency, or other objectives.

This computation is an order of magnitude more complex than computing a point-to-point path. Different objective functions yield different trees: minimizing the total cost of all links in the tree yields a Steiner tree (an NP-hard problem), while minimizing the cost to reach each leaf individually is faster but yields different results. Not all routers in the network can perform branching, adding additional constraints that must be checked.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding the best way for one sender to reach many receivers is much harder than finding a path to one receiver. The complexity grows quickly as the number of destinations increases.

sections.title: Why Routers Cannot Do This Alone
sections.content:
Computing a least-cost-to-leaf P2MP tree requires roughly the same processing as computing one optimal point-to-point path for each leaf in sequence. Computing a Steiner tree requires roughly an order of magnitude more computation. While many routers can perform simple Constrained Shortest Path First (CSPF) calculations for point-to-point paths, they quickly become overloaded with multiple such calculations, such as during failure recovery.

Overloading a router with P2MP path computation diverts its processing power from other critical tasks: servicing point-to-point LSP setup requests, maintaining routing protocol state, and forwarding packets. This can damage the router's ability to recover from network faults and disrupt existing traffic. Additionally, ingress routers for P2MP LSPs are typically ordinary routers without special hardware, so requiring them to compute P2MP paths is not a practical solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular routers do not have enough computing power for this task, and spending all their power on one path computation means they cannot handle new requests or maintain the network.

sections.title: PCE Deployment Models for P2MP
sections.content:
The RFC describes two main PCE deployment approaches. Offline computation is performed ahead of time, typically by a management application planning long-lived LSPs or recovery responses. This approach works well for stable, long-term paths and gives network operators full control over placement. Online computation is performed on demand when routers need paths. A dedicated PCE server, a high-capacity router, or even a management system can perform online computation; multiple PCEs may cooperate to handle requests.

Online computation has several variants. A PCE may compute an entire P2MP tree in response to a request from the ingress router. Alternatively, it may compute only the first fragment of the tree (from the ingress to intermediate branch points), leaving other PCEs to compute the subsequent subtrees. This tree fragmentation approach reduces the computational burden on any single PCE and is particularly useful in multi-domain networks where different domains operate their own PCEs.
sections.plainLanguage: Either plan paths in advance using a management tool, or ask a special high-powered computer to compute them on the spot. For very complex networks, split the computation across multiple planning computers.

sections.title: Operational Scenarios
sections.content:
Reoptimization and modification are important for P2MP LSPs. When a leaf is removed, the tree is automatically pruned (no computation needed). When a new leaf is added, only a simple branch-point selection and path computation is required. However, repeated additions and removals leave the tree sub-optimal, requiring full reoptimization. Such reoptimization can be performed as a background task and may be split across subtrees to reduce per-PCE load.

Repair and failure recovery differ for P2MP paths. A single network fault typically affects only a subset of the total leaf set, so repair need not recompute the entire tree—it only needs to compute new branches to reconnect the affected leaves. This is computationally simpler and faster than full reoptimization. Disjoint paths for protection add further computational complexity. Computing link-disjoint P2P paths is already non-trivial; computing disjoint P2MP paths is considerably harder and represents a scenario where PCE offload is particularly valuable.
sections.plainLanguage: When a destination leaves or joins, only part of the tree changes. When the network breaks, only affected branches need repair, not the whole tree. Computing backup paths for protection is very hard and should definitely go to the special computer.

sections.title: Design and Manageability
sections.content:
The PCE architecture supports capability advertisement, allowing routers to discover which PCEs can perform P2MP computations and what objective functions they support (some PCEs may support least-cost-to-leaf but not Steiner trees). The architecture also allows priority-based request queuing: if a PCE becomes overloaded, point-to-point computation requests can be prioritized over P2MP requests. PCEs can redistribute overload by delegating computation requests to less-burdened peers using PCE cooperation mechanisms.

From a network operation standpoint, PCE computation of P2MP paths enables more dynamic network behavior than traditional management-based planning: participants can be dynamically added and removed, trees can be reoptimized as network conditions change, and failure recovery can proceed automatically. However, P2MP computations consume more CPU and bandwidth than P2P computations per request, so networks must be sized with sufficient PCE capacity and authentication mechanisms must be used to prevent denial-of-service attacks from spurious computation requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The system lets routers ask 'Can you handle this kind of computation?' and handles overload by splitting work among multiple planners. It enables flexible networks that adapt when users join, leave, or network problems occur.
